Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 55, to amend the Winding-up Act. He said: The purpose of the Bill is merely to correct an anomaly that exists. The Supreme Court of Ontario includes two divisions- the High Court of Justice, and the Court of Appeal. All the rules of practice, generally speaking, are made by the entire court, comprising the two divisions. The provision in the Winding-up Act defines the court in the province of Ontario as the High Court of Justice, and confides to that court the making of the rules. The result is that, whereas all other rules of practice are made by the entire court, comprising the two divisions, the rules under the Winding-up Act are made by only one division of the court. This is anomalous, and it is on the suggestion of the Chief Justice of Ontario, with, I understand, the concurrence of the other judges of both divisions of the court, that we seek to amend the Act, so as to put the rules under the Winding-up Act in the same position as all other rules of practice in the Courts of Ontario.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for a committee to inquire into purchases of shells or other munitions or goods by/the Shell Committee, resumed from Tuesday, March 7.

Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the House for a short time in order to conclude the remarks which I have to address to the House upon this very important resolution. I had covered, before midnight on Tuesday, the most important points raised by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), and most of the reasons given by him why this resolution should not carry. I desire to refer to a few more, and then I shall be through.
Just before adjournment I was discussing the question of fuses. I had described, as generally as I possibly could and yet to make it intelligible, the construction of a fuse and the manner of its operation. On a former occasion I stated in this House that the Shell Committee had given two contracts to firms in the United States. One was to the American Ammunition Company of New York for 833,334 fuses at $4.50 each, and 1,666,666 at $4 each. This, figured out, made a total of $10,416,667. Then, they gave another contract to the International Arms and Fuse Company of New York for 833,334 fuses at $4.50 each, and for 1,666,666 at the same price, making a total of $11,250,000. In other words, we have here contracts for almost $22,000,000 given to firms in the United States. When we find contracts of that immensity given to our neighbours, we naturally commence to. ask, why is it that the Canadian manufacturers could not have produced these necessary articles? A fuse is not a very big article; it cannot be the size of it that prevents the Canadian manufacturer from making it. It is only made of brass, a little copper and a few steel springs. The steel springs are so minute that a few thousand pounds of them would be all that would be necessary for the whole 5,000,000 fuses. It cannot be for lack of machinery, because we can get machinery in Canada that will make anything. It certainly cannot be for lack of workmen, because it has been demonstrated during the last year or two that Canadian workmen can make shells and anything else

in the line of warlike supplies, and therefore I believe they can make fuses. Why is it? This Shell Committee was organized away back in September, or October, 1914, and it was not until the summer of 1915, or until pretty nearly a year had gone by, at least nine months, before these gentlemen even commenced, as far as the public are advised, to consider the question of fuses. I pointed out on Tuesday the absolute uselessness of shells unless you had fuses to explode them; and yet these gentlemen sit around taking contracts unto themselves and giving contracts unto their neighbours, friends, and associates, entirely disregarding the whole question of fuses, which is the very life of the transaction, and without which every dollar expended is absolutely thrown away.
When we come to investigate this question, we arrive at some most remarkable conclusions. I have not had time thoroughly to digest all the remarks made by the Minister of Militia, but I think I am correct when I say that he stated very near the close of the debate on Tuesday evening that the graze fuse, or the fuse that he calls the No. 100, is being made in England to-day for $1.95. I proved to him out of his own records-I took no garbled reports or anything of that kind-that from 1909 down to 1914 he bought exactly the same fuse, the No. 100, or graze fuse, from firms in England, from Vickers & Co. on a contract, a quantity of something like 25,000, at $2.26 each. He says that they are being manufactured in England to-day for $1.95 each. After spending nine months of precious time, and taking chances of the British army being annihilated for lack of ammunition, this Shell Committee gave a contract in the United States for 1,666,666 of these fuses, not at $1.95 each as in Britain, not at $2.26, the same as was paid for the same article just one year before, but at $4; that is they paid $3,000,000 more than these fuses could have been bought for in England at that time. I have positive information here as to the price of the T & P fuse, or the timefuse, as it is called. I find he bought these fuses for $2.26 each in Britain. I see that he gave contracts in the United States for 2,500,000 and 833,000 of these time-fuses at $4.50, although he had bought the very same fuse in Britain a year before for $2.26. I have proof of that right from his own documents. Why is it necessary to pay such an enormous premium as this in order to get these very necessary articles? If the minister said that he could not get them in Britain, that might be an answer. But he has not said so, and he won't say so, 98
because he can't say so. He has not said that they could not be made in Canada, because that would not be true, and I know the Minister of Militia would be the last man to state what was not true. In the month of June last a contract was given to the Russell Motor Car Company, of Toronto-if the contract was not in their name it was given to that company ar way-for 500,000 graze fuses; half of thcee fuses were to be supplied at $4 each, and the other half at $3 each. So the minister was able to get fuses manufactured in Canada for $3.50 each, and that on a small contract of 500,000. Yet he placed a contract in the United States for 1,666,666 fuses, and paid $4 each for them. Will any hon. gentleman in this House who attempts to defend these transactions say that these fuses could not be made in Canada?
We had an almost unpleasant exchange of compliments across the floor of this House on Tuesday evening last, because in my judgment the Minister of Militia did not do himself justice. He tried to get behind the quibble that no fuses had been furnished the Shell Committee, and no contract made by the present Munitions Board. But it turned out that what he meant to say was that fuses had been furnished to the Shell Committee, and, that they had made contracts. The Shell Committee made a contract with the Russell Motor ' Car Company, and that company have manufactured fuses in Canada, and are manufacturing them to-day. Only yesterday I saw Mr. T. A. Russell, and he told me they were carrying out their contract, and delivering more than 3,500 fuses a day. He said that they would, not only be able to fill their contract, but fill it ahead of time, after complying with every condition and requirement. And yet these Americans who got this enormous contract at this horrible price have never furnished a solitary fuse,, and the British Empire might have been smashed to pieces by the German armies if it had relied on the Canadian Shell Committee to supply fuses for their shrapnel and high explosive shells.
Why is it that they had to go to the United States? You have to go to New York to find, out. I am sorry I have not been there many times myself in the last year, but there are many people in Canada who have. And it all comes back to the same dirty trail-J. Wesley Allison. Every dirty trail in the whole transaction leads to Allison, and there is not a



dirty trail' that J. Wesley Allison has not trodden in the last year and a half. This is the gentleman who is playing sick down in New York; the man who has pneumonia, according to the newspapers; the man who, for the last three nights, including last night, has taken a seat in a Pullman from New York to Canada, and had his grips stowed away on board by the porter, and then just before the train pulled out, has sneaked out by the back door and gone back to his hotel. He thinks somebody is watching him, and he is quite right. He is trying to put people off the scent; he does not want us to know where he is. But we know where he is all right, and we know who will be closeted with him to-morrow morning about eight o'clock. We know there was an hon. gentleman of this House who was very brave here on Tuesday evening,-simply dyifig to jump into the breach. He could not wait until this afternoon to answer the remarks I was making. He is the man who is primarily responsible for all these nefarious transactions, perhaps more responsible than any of Kis colleagues. This man, who has not the manhood to stand up here and answer these charges, and who, when brought face to face with the untrue statements made by him, and made advisedly and deliberately-
The hon. gentleman is certainly going too far. It is out of order to say that an hon, member of this House deliberately made an untrue statement.

I gladly withdraw that expression. It was this man who told us that the prices of shells in Britain were greater than the prices in Canada, and I have proved that every word he said in that connection was not true in fact. This is the man who is not here to-day to answer these charges, but finds it necessary to go to Montreal to address some sort of a meeting before the board of trade, and then go south for his health. This is the hon. gentleman who will be consorting with J. Wesley Allison to-morrow morning in New York, and they will be consorting with a lot more of their ilk in the next few days, down in the balmy atmosphere of Florida. This hon. gentleman leaves it to somebody else to defend these transactions, and the man who attempts to do it has certainly got a thankless task. This J. Wesley Allison, who the Minister of Militia says has saved this country and

the Allies $50,000,000 in the purchase of munitions, is the man who, along with Carnegie, a member of the Shell Committee- and I want to bring him in because he is just as responsible as Allison; he was in New York consorting with these gentlemen just as much as Allison was-these two gentlemen went to the United States, representing the Shell Committee, and made the nefarious transactions I have described with these American firms; firms who had never manufactured a fuse before, who never intended to manufacture a fuse, and who have never manufactured a fuse to this day. These firms sublet the contracts to other contracting firms, of which J. Wesley Allison is a member, at prices which will net millions and millions to them. And then they come back to the Canadian Parliament, and say: "You have no right to investigate transactions of this kind; you are disloyal; you are not good Canadians; if you ask to have these matters investigated and brought out in the light of day, you are not good Britishers."
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that if there is anything in the whole history of Canada which ought to have the light of day shed on it, it is the transactions of the Shell Committee with regard to fuses. I have not told one-half of the iniquity. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition gave the beginning of it in his address on Tuesday, when he said that before these contracts were consummated, or even entered into, the Shell Committee advanced to these American gentlemen over $3,000,000. This money was advanced before a blow was struck, and hon. gentlemen opposite say that it was necessary to advance this money in order to get the firms organized and doing business. They did not tell the Russell Motor Car Company of Toronto that they had advanced to these American firms $3,000,000, or nearly 15 per cent of the contract. I am told, however-I did not get this from Mr. Russell-that when the Canadian manufacturers found out that the Shell Committee had advanced this enormous sum-to American manufacturers, they went to the Shell Committee and that committee was compelled to give them an advance in order to help to finance the work. The result is that the Canadian manufacturers are furnishing the fuses, exactly as per contract, for $3.50 each, whereas the American manufacturers, who have received over $3,000,000 of good British and Canadian money, have never furnished a fuse, but have simply sublet the contracts

to the friends and confreres of J. Wesley Allison, and I do not think, Sir, you would have to make half a dozen guesses in order to name his principal confrere.
Now, Sir, why could not fuses be made in Canada? A fuse consists simply of between twenty and twenty-five pieces of brass which have to be turned to certain shapes and certain sizes and which must measure up to a certain gauge. Every watchmaker in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, is in a position to do something toward manufacturing these fuses. Of these twenty to twenty-five different parts one is a little ball, another is a little pin, another a disc, another an oval, and so on, and they need not all be made in one factory. The Munitions Board, if they would mobilize the industries of this country, could have, not one factory, not twenty factories, but a hundred, yes, five hundred places in Canada where fuses could be made to-day, and in that way they would be able to give work to thousands and tens of thousands of Canadians who are idle at present and who would be glad to have an opportunity of earning a livelihood. The Minister of Militia is always speaking about the manufacturers. Why does he not do something with the manufacturers in regard to the making of fuses? Why does he not put tens of thousands of people in a position to earn their livelihood in an honest way, by doing something to aid this country in bringing this war to a successful issue? It is no wonder the Minister of Militia is not here this afternoon to reply, to these statements.
I was also very much surprised at the attempt made by the right hon. Prime Minister to make the people of this country believe that my right hon. leader and myself and every other hon. gentleman on this side who have discussed this question, were having a fling at the manufacturers of Canada and were trying to prevent them from doing a legitimate business. [DOT] I would like any hon. gentleman opposite to point his fipger at one statement that I have made against the Canadian manufacturers making shells, fuses, clothing, and everything else which could possibly be used in the conduct of this war. I would like him to point his finger at one such statement made by any hon. member on this side of the House. We find fault to-day with the Shell Committee because of the prices which they have given to some of the manufacturers for making these various articles. I have commended them; I do now commend them for many things that they have
done. I made the statement a month ago; I repeated it on Tuesday last; I repeat it now: that if the only company capable of doing this work consists of the Prime Minister, let them give the contract to the Prime Minister, let them give it to the man who can do the work quickest and best; let them give it to the company which can turn out the finished article in the shortest possible time.
I have made a list of some things for which I can commend the Shell Committee. By going over some notes that I have been able, with a good deal of difficulty, to prepare, I find that up to the month of January last when the minister made his speech on the Address-and it is as of that date I am now speaking-orders had been given for the manufacture of about 11,000,000 18-pr. shrapnel shells; that at that time there had been delivered to the Shell Committee about 5,750,000, and that the Shell Committee were able to find in Canada fifteen firms capable of doing pretty nearly .three-quarters of that work and they did pretty nearly that amount. This friction tube consists of a square block about two inches long, filled with some material like that on the outside of matchboxes. A piece of metal goes inside, with a surface like a file, or rasp, and when you pull out the file it lights the match. There is a tube about an inch and a half long that goes down the breach of the gun into the powder; the fire goes down the hole, explodes the cordite, and the gun is fired. Though opposed by the' Government, the motion carried by a majority of 157. The Aberdeen Ministry immediately resigned. Lord Palmerston formed a new Government with little change in its personnel. Speaking of the difficulty of getting witnesses to give evidence Mr. Roebuck said:
I feel corruption about me, but I oannot place my hand on it.
Mr. Roebuck did not make charges, he honestly admitted the difficulty of getting evidence, but he said: I feel corruption' about me. I have taken a little more time than I intended to, but I want for a moment to summarize very briefly the salient points of the situation as it stands to-day. My honoured leader has asked this House to grant a committee to investigate the conduct of the Shell Committee in carrying on the business transactions entrusted to it since the beginning of the war in 1914. The Prime Minister refuses that, because he says it is not in the interest of the public that these matters should be investigated during the war, and it is not following the precedent laid down in Great Britain during the Crimean War and the Boer War of 1899-1902. If you accept the truthfulness of the citations which I have just read, you will see that they absolutely shatter the last contention and common sense, decency and the ambition for honest Government in Canada absolutely shatter the former contention. Because something happened ten years ago, or fifty years ago, is not a good reason why, under another condition of affairs, we should not investigate things here to-day. Are we always to be tied to the apron-strings of somebody, have we no initiative, have we not the right to investigate our own affairs because in past days somebody has done something else? Surely the Conservative party can furnish some better argument than that, in order to show that there ought not to be an investigation into these transactions. Then, I promised you, Mr. Speaker, that I would try and give you some additional reasons why this committee should be granted.

time they have an opportunity of telling the Prime Minister so. This is its proud record. While Canada's men were bleeding on the fields of Flanders, Sir Robert Borden delivered a brave oration in London, saying what Canada would do : " The whole-power of the nation must he consecrated to the task." Invited by the British authorities to begin consecrating the power of the nation by organizing the National Transcontinental railway shops for national- service, the Dominion Government at first consented. Then after being publicly thanked in Montreal hy Mr. Lloyd George's representative, Canada's Government failed to live up to its word. Instead of the whole power of the nation being consecrated to the task, the only national shop in use is one placed at the disposal of one more private profiteering group ... so private that the country is not even told the names of the profiteers in possession at Transcona.
So, the Dominion Government has chosen. Shell profiteering is to be defended and shielded by the responsible leaders in the Federal House of Commons. The whole power of the nation, and all its flowing oratory and sophistry is to be consecrated to the task of defending war loot. But does the Dominion Government truly represent the spirit of the Canadian people?
Sir, that is the question I ask. Does the attitude of the Canadian Government to-day truly represent the spirit of the Canadian people? If this thing was all right, why is the old Shell Committee not at work to-day? What sent Mr. Lloyd George's representative over here in the month of July, 1915, if the British Government were satisfied with the condition of affairs on that date? If this Shell Committee was acting honestly and uprightly and above board, and if this Government was doing its whole duty, do you suppose that Mr. Thomas would have been sent over here? When he came to Ottawa, did he not have-

a delicate mission to perform? Can you imagine a man handling a delicate subject with greater diplomacy than did Mr. Thomas? He had to say in effect to the Government of Canada:	" The committee
that you have appointed have fallen down; they have not been straight and honest with the Government; they have charged two prices for shells and everything else, and' the British Government must kick them out. We want to do it as politely and decently as possible and with the greatest diplomacy." He remained here for three months, and before he went away they were kicked out. Now, what is the use of asking why they were kicked out? What is the use of the Prime Minister reading extracts from letters written to him by somebody whose name he does not give? What is the use of reading extracts from letters which Mr. Hiehens wrote to him? Mr. Hichens is not the people of Canada; he does not pay a cent of taxes here, nor does he represent one Canadian voter. Would you expect a representative of the Imperial Government to come here to a government to whom they ate looking for favours, whom they are asking to do their duty in carrying on this war to a successful conclusion, and say: "You are a gang of crooks and I am going to put these men out?" Men in high positions do not say such things. But these men were put out just the same. There is no use in trying to argue the thing away, no use in the Prime Mininster reading long extracts from documents, no use in sophistry. The facts are: Mr. Thomas came; Mr. Thomas saw; and the Shell Committee was conquered. That is all there was to it. And the new commission are now in their places, a commission that, I know, is doing infinitely better than the old committee did, a commission which, I hope, will continue to carry on the good work. All I have to say, in conclusion, is this: If the Government will not grant a commission, - and will not allow the people of Canada to learn the inside facts of the transactions of this Shell Committee, this political organization of theirs, then, in the name of Heaven, let them keep their unholy hands off the present Imperial Munitions Board.

Mr. Sneaker, I rise with some diffidence to address the House at this time. I believe that the part of an ordinary member in this great crisis of our country is to assist by kindly suggestion those whose position places upon them the greatest responsibility that has ever fallen to the lot of statesmen
in this Dominion. I cannot for a single moment believe that the discussion which has taken place can assist in any way towards winning the great war in which we are engaged. When I listened to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell)-I say it frankly-I was tempted to reply in kind. But I conceive that I have a larger duty and a greater responsibility; and, although I may do it poorly, I hope to be able to discharge that responsibility in a somewhat different manner from that in which the hon. member has discharged what he believes to be his. I do not usually quote from newspapers, but I am content to leave it to the Ottawa Free Press of this evening to summarize the speech of the hon. member for Carleton. I do not think that any other language could more fitly describe it:
The speech of Mr. Carvell was of the kind which in recent years have become a habit with him. "We are not making charges against the Government," he said, adding, " no one is saying, either, that any member of the Shell Committee stole anything." Yet, in the next breath, he made the amazing assertion that " the whole trend of the Prime Minister's speech had been that the prime object of the Shell Committee was the distribution of patronage," and that "the members of the Shell Committee had placed enormous orders with themselves at exorbitant prices, and to keep the prices up for themselves they had to give these same prices to all other companies which got contracts."
Mr. Carvell has become a past master in the art of using half truths to make them appear as gospel; but this game, when long continued, grows tiresome, and achieves its own undoing. A comparison of the speeches of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Carvell on the same day tempts one to remark that " fools step in where angels fear to tread." If indulgence in reckless and irresponsible condemnation of opponents is an essential to political partisanship, there are not wanting tens of thousands of Canadians, especially just now, who will pray to be freed from political partisanship. Liberalism as expounded by a Carvell in indeed a fearsome thing.
Will the hon. gentleman read what the same editorial has to say about the Prime Minister?

I leave that delightful task to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdpnald), who seems to have been able, since Tuesday evening, to induce his hon. friend from Carleton to believe that Mr. Thomas Cantley's hands at least are clean. For it will be noticed that while on Tuesday Mr. Thomas Cantley was worthy of condemnation for awarding orders to himself, to-day the hon. member has learned that Mr. Thomas Cantley was in England. I hope he has not overlooked that fact.
The hon, gentleman need, not avoid the question. I asked the hon. member if he would read from the same editorial what is said about the Prime Minister.

I am delighted to see such a manifestation of temper on H- part of the hon. member; it is always amusing and sometimes interesting.
I leave the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton at that, except for one further observation. He has stated that it would be a good thing for Canada if the Government could be changed at this time. I do not believe that the Liberalism of the province in which I reside is represented by an observation such as that. The thousands of young Canadians who have left Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba to fight for this Empire at this time are not actuated by political motives, and not concerned about what party is in power, but they are infinitely concerned about the conduct of the war and the success of our arms on the plains of France and Flanders. It ill becomes any man to talk- about a political truce with one breath, and to talk of the defeat of the Government with another. I do not believe that the genius of Liberalism is reflected by such arrant hypocrisy; I do not believe that such cant adequately expresses the mind of the Canadian people, or of Liberalism, or of the members of the Liberal party throughout Canada. But I do believe that, east, west, north, and south respectable, sober-minded Liberals, whose opinions are not voiced by the scavenging observations of the member for Carleton, believe that our first duty, our paramount duty, our prayerful duty, is to see that this war is carried to a successful conclusion. But when men prate and talk about political "truce" and "neutrality," and then give voice to observations and sentiments such as those expressed by the hon. member for Carleton, it is no wonder that you read editorials such as that in the Ottawa Free Press; it is no wonder that people are praying" to he delivered from such hypocrisy and cant as characterizes the observations of that hon. gentleman.
I desire to direct the attention of the House for a few moments to the official attitude of the Liberal party as distinguished from what may be called its semi-official attitude as shown in the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton. I am not one of those who believe that it is impossible for Liberalism to share with us

the responsibilities and the burdens of this war. I have seen enough of the war to be impressed with it as the most serious and solemn thing that a man ever thought about. Nothing has ever made a like impression on my mind; nothing, I believe, will ever make such an impression on my mind.
On August 19 last, the right hon. leader of the Opposition, from his seat in this House, said:
Speaking for those who sit around me, speaking for the wide constituencies which we represent in this House, I hasten to say that to all these measures we are prepared to give immediate assent. If in what has been done or in what remains to be done there may be anything which in our judgment should not be done or should be differently done, we raise no question, we take no exception, we offer no criticism, and we shall offer no criticism so long as there is danger at the front.
Sir, since this debate commenced, at least
1,000	women have become widows; 10,000 children have become orphans, and before the fortresses of Verdun the greatest danger that has menaced the French Republic since the battle of the Marne, is now imminent. The danger at the front that the right hon. gentleman spoke bf is still with us. I ask him, as a great patriot, as one with wide knowledge of our constitution, and having behind him the longest political history of any man who sits in this House, once more to assert that wholesome doctrine, that great truth which he upheld when on August 19, 1914, he made those observations.
I go further. When in December of that year the right hon. gentleman spoke before the Montreal Reform Club, he used these words:
As soon as war was declared we thought it was part of the duty we owed, not only to our policy, but also to our country, to lay down, for the time being, all party discussions, and to give our whole thought and energy to the new problems which were brought by the war, and not in any way embarass the Government, but on the contrary to facilitate its duty which this new situation created for the Government.
Noble language, lofty sentiments, high ideals of great responsibilities and of splendid patriotism. But how are they being carried out this day by the party that sits opposite? In view of the fact that thousands of men are laying down their lives to-day for the cause of liberty, I ask whether or not hon. gentlemen opposite are endeavouring to embarrass the hands of this 'Government by the "piffle" they are talking-no other word adequately describes the language of hon. gentlemen opposite.

The right hon. leader of the Opposition, speaking before the Ontario Federation of Liberal Clubs on May 21st last, said:
Let the Prime Minister and his colleagues say that there shall he no election as long as the war shall go on, and I will pledge myself and the party, that we shall stop all preparations and think of nothing hut the war.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman
says, " Hear, hear," while from the basement of this building tons of political literature are to-day being sent throughout Canada by the Liberal party organization. Already this session 4,000 columns of Hansard have been filled with the bitterest attacks that have been levelled against any Administration .since Confederation; the most virulent and violent attacks that, I think, you vwill find in the pages of any Hansard. Night after night, day after day; in the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne, in the Budget; attack after attack against the Government, the whole forces of Liberalism, with many noteworthy exceptions, have been hurled against this Administration. Then this party ammunition is being sent out to the electors, and for what purpose? It is designed to endeavour to solidify plastic public opinion against this Administration, while the Administration, all through the day, all through the long watches of night,
. is endeavouring to fight the Huns. While we are being fought from within, the foe is still without. While this Administration is night and day striving to meet the great difficulties that have arisen by reason of this war; while men are assuming responsibilities as large as ever fell to the lot of men, hon. gentlemen opposite are sending out literature, charging, by half-truths and idle insinuations, -that the trusted servants of the people are derelict to their trust and guilty of the highest crimes and misdemeanors. Is that a party truce? Is that the kind of truce of which hon. gentlemen opposite speak? Is that the kind of assistance that the right hon. leader of the Opposition purposes to give to the Government of the day? Is that the method he would employ to avoid embarassing the Government? Is that what high-minded statecraft and noble patriotism inspires in any man? I leave the problem with the people of this great Dominion. I believe that at this time the people are not interested in the differences between Conservatives and Liberals. Speaking for the community in *which I reside, and the province in which
I make my home, I say that men whether they be Liberals or Conservatives have forgotten the signs and nomenclature of party-ism. I wish I could visualize to this House the situation as I see it. No language that I can use would picture the gravity of the situation as it appears to me; no words by which I am capable of giving expression to the thought that is in my nnind could for one moment present the picture as I see it. We idly discuss fiscal questions, while the real problem is whether it will be in our power when the war is over to determine what our fiscal policy shall be. We talk of woman's franchise; how do we know that the Parliament that sits here will be the Parliament of a British people? We waste our time in dealing with questions upon the Order Paper, resolutions here and there, asking something to embarrass an individual or a minister while, Sir, these ministers may not be the ministers of the Crown of Britain to-morrow.

Have no fear on that
point.

I have no fear of the
ultimate end of this great war, but I am concerned as I have never been concerned about anything in my life as to what may happen before that great end is achieved.
What is going on in France to-5 p.m. day? A few months ago I saw
Paris in black, as I had never seen black before. I saw the women of France working in the fields tilling the soil, while their fathers, their sons, and their husbands were doing battle in the trenches. I saw 5,000 French horse, foot and artillery march by, going to face death. I saw 4,000 of the very best of my fellow-Canadians salute the Prime Minister of Canada as they went by in the dusk to the trenches. And when I think of the multiplication of the loss to the state of the men that are dying, of the blood that is being spilled, of the economic waste that is going on; when I see the best men of the Empire being drained from it; when I see the population of the province in which I live being lessened day after day by the departure of men who are so willingly, so gladly, so nobly, so patriotically giving their services for the cause of freedom, I ask myself: where will it end? Sir, we may win a great war, and we may lose an Empire. The discussions the dissensions, the talk such as went on to-day from the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell)-are the things that bring about that very end. He talked to-day in

this House about the war that we were asked to go into, or coaxed to go into. Sir, this is as much a war of the Canadian people as it is of those who live in the city of London or in the city of Paris.
I made no statement that we were asked or coaxed to go into this war. My hon. friend certainly misunderstood me, because I made no such statement; I think he ought to withdraw the remark.
If the hon. gentleman did not say it, Hansard will properly indicate what he did say. My understanding of it was that he said we were asked to go into this war.
I never said such a thing.
If I thought that I had done my hon. friend an injustice, I should certainly not hesitate to withdraw the remark.
I made no such statement; on the contrary, I said that it was our duty to go into this war, and to help win it.

And it is. I should like to make it clear that according to my conception of the situation, there are three lines of defence for Canada. The first line of defence lies out yonder at Verdun; the second line of defence is with the reserves at Shorncliffe and Bramshott; the third line of defence is the reserves in the training camps throughout this Dominion. And just as surely as the freedom and liberty of the men of France and Belgium are at stake, it is my profound conviction that my liberty and my freedom, the institutions under which I live, and the civilization that has been created by the races to which we belong are at issue right here in Canada. When I speak of the noble sentiments of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), I know it was not easy for him, or for those who support him, to express those views. It is not easy for a man holding different views from the Government, having intense political convictions in a democracy such as this, to readily give utterance to those noble sentiments, for they were noble sentiments; they breathed the spirit of the purest patriotism; they are the very noblest and highest sentiments that man can hold. I repeat: it was not easy. During the long years in which he has done so much to shape the public thought and opinion of this Dominion, from

his youth up, my right hon friend has held a political philosophy that looked, ultimately perhaps to that theory of the great French philosopher who saw in this Dominion a land of new republics or independent states. It was a view that men might properly hold, and yet, with the first blast of war, so spontaneous and general was the response of a great people to the cry of the Empire, to the sob of the mother overseas, that my right hon. friend recast for himself, and for those who sit about him, his political creed and political faith, and declared, as I expected, and, in fact, knew he would: that it was the duty of all men who called themselves Canadians to associate themselves at such a time with the Government, and to do their part in preserving our civilization. It was not easy, I say, to discharge the duty which in such a magnificent manner he discharged for himself and his party.
Let us go a step further, and see what we have now. I cannot possibly think for a single moment that the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) reflects the opinion or the spirit of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). By his long and patriotic history, by his long and noble career, I do in all seriousness appeal to the right hon. gentleman to say again in this House that he is content-for the reasons which have been urged upon him so strongly by the Prime Minister in no aeriminious or partisan spirit-to say what he would have done in this crisis had he been Prime Minister. I feel absolutely certain that he would say to this House, as he said when the comparatively trifling war in South Africa was on: we can wait a bit for the consideration of comparatively petty things. He would use more graceful language, but that- the substance of it would be: we can wait a bit, there is surely no hurry to hold up to shame and execration the names of our fellow Canadians who are suspected by political antagonists of doing wrong. I trust he is not one of those who rejoice in the vilification of his fellows and in the slander of Canadians; I trust that that is reserved for the hon. gentleman from Carleton (Mr. Carvell). Sir, I believe the right hon. gentleman had he been Prime Minister, would have said that when this war is over, great problems must arise for solution; thiat there must be inquiry into the whole conduct of the war, whether it affects the Australians in Gallipoli, the Canadians at Ypres, the British at Mons,

or the French on the Marne; that there must be by all the Governments, who are taking 'part in this war, official inquiry that will take cognizance of every action, of the general conduct of affairs, whether in the field or in the office, whether in regard to administrative or to operative affairs.
I believe he would say that with the end of the war must come great constitutional changes, a new statue for Canadians, for Australians, for New Zealanders, equality of citizenship under the flag, great social and economic problems to engage the best attention of the best minds of this Empire.
I feel that that is what my right hon. friend would have said, and gladly said, if he were Prime Minister to-day, and I am certain it is what his followers should join with him in saying: Wait until this war is over, and then we will take stock of all the charges made against individuals and companies, and we will punish them as they deserve.
There has never been a war since the earliest days, in which there were not men who took advantage of their country's necessities to improve their own opportunities. It has been so in the past, and it will always be so. I recall that in the reign of Queen Anne one of the great commanders in chief of the British forces was not beyond doing business for' himself at the expense of the public. The military genius of that man made him one of the great men of history, and yet he took advantage of his country's necessities to promote . his own financial advancement. It. has always been so, and 1 suppose it will continue to be so. What I suggest is, that had my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) been leading this House, he would have said: I do not propose at this juncture to enter into inquiries, but I will leave them, quoting the words of Mr. Asquith and Mr. Balfour in the Boer war: until the war is substantially over, until by the proper perspective we can understand the situation, punish where crimes have been committed, and give reward and praise where men have nobly discharged their duties. And, I say, that there are in this Dominion to-day poor men and women who have not been sparing in their activities, and who have honourably discharged duties to the state, without receiving recognition or reward. Think of what men and women have done, think of what mothers have done in giving their sons freely, of what fathers have done, pinching and paring in order to give to
the Patriotic and Red Cross funds. We will take more stock of all these things after the war is over. 1 am not defending the Shell Committee, I am not attacking it; but I am going to make the argument that this is not the opportune time to have an inquiry of this character, and I am going to give reasons, in the light of the experience which I gained the last time I was across the Atlantic. I shall conclusively show to this House that at least one investigation that has been carried on since the war began did not good to the Canadian people, but on the contrary did them incalculable injury.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite speak of ministers of the Crown as though they lived on a bed of roses. Does any man, for a single moment, think that the duties and responsibilities that have devolved upon the Prime Minister since the war began are lightly to be undertaken or easily to be discharged? I have had many differences with the Minister of Militia, but I do say that no man has more energetically or tirelessly discharged the duties of his office than General Sir Sam Hughes. He has been attacked by men who may have had some reason for their attack, but I say, whatever may have been his faults, that he at least has been a dynamo of human energy, and he has been able, by reason of his great and tireless energy, to accomplish that which men of calmer minds, of more equable temperament and less energy, might have failed to accomplish. I state that publicly in this House, because I think it is fairly due to him.
Does this House forget what took place last year? Does this House remember that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, in the midst of the -war, discharged what 1 believe was the most painful duty that ever fell to the lot of a Prime Minister in Canada? Naipe me an occasion during fifteen years of piping times of peace when any such duty was discharged by the predecessor of Sir Robert Borden in the office of Prime Minister. Be it an Arctic expedition, a Yukon scandal, a failure to give Parliament the names of the shareholders of the North Atlantic Trading Company, stolen ballots enabling a man to sit in this House' who- had no right to sit here, or timber 'scandals, was any punishment ever meted out to those who were guilty? Yet, in the midst of this war, the Prime Minister performed, the most painful duty that, in my judgment, ever fell to the lot of a Prime Minister of Canada. And he did it because it was in



keeping with what he thought it was right to do, and it was in line with the principles expressed by him, that if it was suggested that a crime or fraud had been committed, it was his duty to see that this crime was exposed and punishment meted out. If there is one thing more than another, which places the Prime Minister high in the estimation of this House and of the country, it is the part my right hon. friend took, when, regardless of feeling, of sentiment, of all those ties that bind party leaders to their followers, he stood out as the great Canadian that he is, and declared that there would be no graft or corruption within his party during this war. If. there is one thing more than another which will always be a matter of pride to me, it is not the noble achivements of our Canadians upon the field of battle-I knew they would acquit themselves well-but the fact that at this time we have at the head of the Government a man of sufficient moral character and force to stand in his place and repudiate two of his followers, a thing that has never been done before in the Canadian Parliament. I commend the Prime Minister's high conception of duty, as being Worthy to rank alongside the achievements of our brave Canadians on the battlefield.
Does the hon. gentleman not think that it might be possible that he sacrificed his followers in order to save the head of the Government?

The hon. gentleman suggests that possibly the high-minded action of the Prime Minister was taken for the purpose of saving himself, but I have not seen any evidence of cowardice upon the part of the Prime Minister in dealing with questions of this kind. Possibly the hon. gentleman had in mind an episode that happened in his own county of Prescott, and possibly he thought that Mr. Rowell dic^ something of a like kind for the purpose of saving his own head.
May I now point out that as Canadiaiis we have taken part in this war voluntarily and gladly. I aim not here to-day to speak of the part that our noble Canadians have taken upon the battlefield. Some of them will unfortunately return no more, but their memories will be blessed down through the years, and their example will lead men to nobler thoughts and higher ideals of public service and public life. I heard it from the lips of the great Commander in Chief of the French Forces, I heard it from every one who was present

to judge, that Canada had saved the day in that great battle that took place nearly a year ago, nor is there question as to the noble achievements of our fellow British subjects from Australia. Gallipoli will live as long as history is written and read. What was done by the Guards division will ever live in the traditions of the British service as the embodiment of all that is glorious. We Canadians are sharers in that glory; we are participants in these great achievements.
But, Sir, there is another ground upon which I should like to consider the position of Canadians. What has been our attitude in relation to finance, internal development, and the conduct of the war from the standpoint of administration? Have we less cause to be proud in the one case than in the other? We raised a great internal loan, twice what was asked; and we are now financing the operations of the British Government and stabilizing and adjusting exchange. We have been enabled by an appropriate campaign in reference to production, to ensure the largest crop that has ever been reaped by the tillers of the soil; we have been able to keep our people fairly employed, but more, we have been enabled to show an adaptability, and a skill in invention and achievement, which have challenged the admiration of our Allies, and I doubt not of the enemy as well. I should like this House to understand the greatness of these achievements. I did not realize how great they were until I heard men, who were competent to express an opinion, piay tribute to Canada. It is not a question of munitions alone. It is a question of wheat, of coal, of flour, of barley, of oats, of hay- it is the great question of the production of all those things that make possible the successful carrying on of the war. This House little realizes that after the war broke out the British Government was confronted with a startling shortage of munitions. Our heavy artillery, even obsolete artillery, rifles, even obsolete rifles, were sent across the Atlantic with all speed and haste. Then what followed? England said to Canada: Can you get us 200,000 shells, 100,000 18-pounders and
100,000	15-pounders. They were told we could do it. They said: Get them for us, get them in the United States, get them somewhere, we do not know where you will get them. Then, that spirit of enterprise, that spirit of pride, that spirit of patriotism that manifests itself equally in achievements in times of peace as in war, asserted itself and the Canadian people
said: we will not only produce you 200,000 18-pounder and 15-pounder shells, but we will undertake to produce ammunition on a large scale to enable this war to be carried on with munitions produced within our own Empire. . This was the idea of Major General Sir Sam Hughes. You may condemn him. you may not agree with him, but when the authorities in Great Britain realized that they were confronted with a practical difficulty, he rose to the occasion and he said: We will not get this ammunition outside of this country, we will get it right in this Dominion, and you will get not only what you want but so much more that you will be surprised. In December last I was in England and I made it my business to get information at first hand both from Ministers of the Crown and from the head of the High Explosives Committee .a gentleman who, as all the members of my profession know, left his place in the Privy Council, and, at the direct invitation of the Prime Minister of Great Britain gave his attention, as the supreme authority upon chemistry to the production of high explosives. I refer to Lord Moulton. I was told that Canada had so far exceeded the expectations of the British people as to cause them to wonder whether or not we really made these munitions in Canada. I was proud then of being a Canadian, I was proud of our achievements industrially as I had been pTOud of the part that Canadians had taken upon the field of battle. Let us view calmly, and not as bitter partisans, what was done.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition on Tuesday last read from the speech of Earl Curzon, Lord Privy Seal, as to what our position was in the matter. I shall not trouble the House by reading it but I shall summarize what he said. He said.: "We made the Canadian Government our agents to name'a committee to buy munitions; we asked the Canadian Government to name a committee to buy munitions for us; the Canadian Government acceded to the request and gave the British Government certain names."
Did it ever occur to this House that the Hudson Bay Company is the purchasing agent in Canada for the French republic, and that since the war began the Canadian Pacific has purchased no inconsiderable quantity of supplies for the British Government? The Hudson Bay Company has also made considerable purchases for the Russian Government, and, to a more limited extent, for the Italian Government. I do 99J
not know, but I doubt not that before the Hudson Bay Company was named, inquiry was made of this Government through the Embassy in London as to whether the Hudson Bay Company was a reputable firm, and that the answer was given in the affirmative. In the case of the Shell Committee the British Government-not knowing Canadians and being unable to tell whether Mr. So and So would be able to do such and such a thing-said to the Canadian Government: "Give us the names of a committee that will serve for this purpose." The leader of the Government, with his Minister of Militia and the Cabinet, said: "We know six, or seven, or ten men of great repute and experience who will admirably suit your purpose." And they named General Bertram, Mr. Carnegie, Mr. Watts, Mr. Cantley

and will the hon. member for Pictou say that his appointment was not a wise one-and other gentlemen; it is not necessary for me to go over the whole list. The British Government said: "We assume that, when you put your imprimatur upon these men, they are fit for the purpose." And so the business was conducted by these gentlemen, in the manner that has been described. Now, that is exactly what happened with reference to the French republic, only that they named the Hudson Bay Company.
Does my hon. friend suggest that the members of the Shell Committee became the appointees of the British Government?
Absolutely.
When they were called! on to resign then, why did they resign to' the Minister of Militia and not to the British Government?

The reason is easily given, and Mr. Hichens gave the ..reason in his letter. The Minister of Militia was the person responsible in the first instance for the appointment of these gentlemen, and naturally they turned in their resignations to the same source. In other words, the Minister of Militia said to General Bertram: "I have named you, and you now become an official of the British Government." The cable that the hon. member for Carleton read distinctly and positively indicates that the committee was acting for the British Government. I may as well read it again. It is found on page 1598 of Hansard:
Reference your cipher September 17 Committee reports price of 100,000 shrapnel 18-pr.

as per your cablegrams and specifications will be $S.55~ each delivered at Montreal, 200,000 by November 1, and at least 30,000 monthly thereafter. Usual inspection charges. Shall we proced? If so, please arrange line of credit through Canadian High Commissipner and in favour of Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, Canada. Specifications 15-pr. just to hand. Price later. Please answer. Committee wait.
The credit itself was an Imperial credit, absolutely. The money was the. money of , Britain, not of Canada.
