That is a body presided over by a gentleman whose name is mentioned, a General Bertram, and upon it are representatives of the various manufacturing interests in the Dominion, and the function of the committee is to advise the minister as to the contracts which, on behalf of the Imperial Government, he shall conclude. All applications are made to him.
The Minister of Militia is the gentleman who concludes the contracts.

I am delighted that my hon. friend has directed the attention of the House to this quotation, because it was only to save time that I did not read it. The minister referred to is the Imperial Minister of Munitions, as the hon. member well knows.
Not at all.

And what is more, the fact is and the records show, that not a single contract for shells was closed between that Shell Committee and a contractor without the cabled consent and advice of the Minister of Munitions in London. The absolute fact is that General Bertram and his committee, as shown by the documents that are now to be found in Hansard, did not close a contract for shrapnel, high explosives, 6-inch, 8-inch, or 9-inch shells, without communication by cable with the Imperial Minister of Munitions and without receiving from him his o.k.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us what Imperial Minister they communicated with before there was a Minister of Munitions?

The Minister of War.
Lord Kitchener, had a branch in his own

department over which General von Donlop, I think presided. Before Lloyd George was made Minister of Munitions, the application's were sent to Lord Kitchener.
There is nothing of that in Lord Curzon's statement.
I have read Lord Curzon's statement, and the minister to whom he refers is the Minister of Munitions in London.
Such an argument would not stand in any court of law.

There need not be any discussion as to what Lord Curzon meant. Let us divest ourselves of all these technical discussions and get down to the facts. The Shell Committee communicated with the Minister of War or the Minister of Munitions, whoever happened to be in charge, first Lord Kitchener, with General von Donop, and later, Mr. Lloyd George. More, over, the facts can be learned by any hon. gentleman opposite by going down to the offices of the Shell Committee and aseer-taining them, and my hon. friend from Carleton, who has been so studious in his examination of the papers in the back room of the Shell Committee, could easily have ascertained the facts.	*

I want to emphatically deny that I have ever been in the back room of the Shell Committee.
Mr. BiENNEITT: The front room, then.
I have never seen the papers, and I do not know anything about them. '

I am bound to accept that statement, but I have it from a member of the Shell Committee that yesterday my hon. friend was perusing the papers of the Shell Committee for the purpose of speaking in this House.

I want my hon. friend to withdraw that statement because it is not true. I never saw any files of papers;
I never went to the Munitions Board to look up files of papers. I went to the Munitions Board to look over shells.

Yesterday?
Mr. CIAR,VELL,: Yes.

Then you were there?
Mr. CARVElLiL: I saw no papers; I perused no files, and I will not allow my hon. friend to make a statement like that without challenging it.	[DOT]

Mr. SPEAKER. Order. According to the rules of the House, the hon. member for Calgary is bound to accept the statement made by fhe hon. member for Carleton.

I accept his statement
gladly. The hon. member says he attended the Shell Committee's office yesterday for the purpose of obtaining information as to the shells.
Exactly.
And doubtless he obtained the information he required.	[DOT]
I did.

And I am perfectly satisfied that if he had pursued his inquiries to the extent he should, he would have found that the Shell Committee concluded no order for shells without communicating with the Imperial Minister of Munitions, or the War Office, as the case might be. I merely mention that in passing.
I desire to point out just one further fact and I have done with that side of the issue. After Mr. Thomas and Mr. Hichens investigated, they made a report which according to a well-defined policy, will not be brought down until after the war is over; but they named a new Imperial Munitions Committee, and what was the personnel of it? My hon. friend, who descanted this afternoon upon the terrible evils of General Bertram and Mr. Carnegie, and who descanted at equal length upon the personnel of the new Munitions Board, overlooked the fact that both Mr. Carnegie and General Bertram are members of that board.

What has General
Bertram done since the new board began work?

He has been doing his
share of the work.

He has been in
Florida.

He may have been in
Florida on account of his health having been injured by the attacks of hon. members opposite. His work has been appreciated by every one else. It may be that, having won the commendation of the British people and having been knighted by his Sovereign, and then denounced by a misguided minority in the Canadian Parliament, he has been compelled to go to another clime for his health, but at the outset he advised the board in their work, and he has gradually got the prices of shells reduced. Mr. Carnegie has been over Canada ; he has been to England doing what he could in presenting the claims of the Canadian manufacturers and people to the Minister of Munitions for the purpose of increasing the number of orders to be received by the Canadian people, to give employment to larger numbers of our workmen, to found new factories and to create new industries in this country. That is what he has been doing. Mr. Carnegie, when he first came to Canada, was a doubting Thomas, who did not believe in the potentialities of this country. Returning to England with the accomplished facts to show for his activity, he comes back to us again with fresh orders. So that, now we have four hundred factories with 136,000 workmen ready to resume work to-morrow at the sound of the whistle, where previously less than 36,000 were employed.
This Munitions Board thus reconstructed, the old committee being honourably discharged, is now charged with the responsibility of carrying forward the work. And now that the old committee is dead, the right hon. leader of the Opposition and his followers propose to hold a post-mortem. They know that they cannot in this way usefully serve the state. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) will not, say that anything a committee of investigation could do by way of post-mortem could in any way assist or serve the state. They know that the iGovernment to whom the committee were answerable, the Govern mant whose servants they were, the ministry in Great Britain, declare that the committee's work has been done to their satisfaction. I say it guardedly, (but I say it emphatically, that these hon. gentle-know that no useful purpose would be served, except one, and that would be described in the language of Beaconsfield when he came back from Berlin-" It might at least serve the purpose of maligning their opponents and vilifying the people of the country in which they live." Let us be frank and fair ,about this. Not only does it serve no useful purpose, but it Pauses great harm. When the hon. member for Carleton this afternoon referred to the fact that a Liberal government should be in power, and that it would give great pleasure to the people, I know the people to whom it would give great pleasure-the -people who occupy the central empires of Europe. They are the ,people who would be pleased, who would be delighted. The enemy whom
I rise to ask a question for information. Was the money that was being deposited to the credit of the Shell Committee deposited by the Government of Canada?

My hon. friend knows that, in the first instance, the credit was wired through the High Commissioner's office, from the Chancellor of the Exchequer to the Deputy Minister of Militia as persona -designate, for the purchase of shells. We made the loan of $ 100,000,000- $50,000,000 more than was asked for-and

that $50,000,000 is being loaned to the British Government to pay for the purchases in Canada. That $50,000,000 is to be lent to the British Government* for the purpose of paying for their purchases in Ganada-hay, oats, wheat, rye, and various other commodities that are bought here, including munitions of war.

With regard to this loan which my hon. friend says is being made to the Imperial Government to pay for munitions, etc., is the money deposited directly to t!he credit of the Shell Committee by the Canadian Government?

My understanding of it is this: the credit is a credit that is arranged for the Imperial Government. Our money is placed to their credit, and then' the Imperial Government advises the Shell Committee as to what their expenditures may be, and as to what money they have avail-, able for checking against.
I understand, then, that the money is put directly to the credit of the Shell Committee by the Canadian Government?

No. The right hon. Chancellor of the Exchequer has arranged a special account for the Imperial Munitions Board, not the Shell Committee. The Imperial Munitions Board gets money from one source, the Imperial Government; and the Imperial Government borrows part of it from the Canadian Government.
I am speaking of the old Shell Committee.

The old Shell Committee went out of business before the Canadian loan was made. On November 20, 1915, the old Shell Committee was superseded by the Imperial Munitions Board, and the credit arranged by the Imperial Government for the old Shell Committee was a credit created by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, transferring the money as such from London to Canada.
Do I understand, then, that no part of the money that was handed to the Shell Committee was placed directly to their credit by the Canadian Government?

No part of it; that is my understanding. It was all Imperial money that they had; the Imperial Government became responsible for finding the money. For instance, let us say that we owed the Imperial Government $2,000,000, and the Imperial Government owed us $2,000,000 100 .
for munitions; book-keeping entries would be made by .way of arranging exchange and saving trouble-that is all. But it must be remembered that in so far as the financial side of it is concerned, the paymaster at the present moment is the British people, not the Canadian people. Tnat is what I want to make clear; let there be no getting away from that point.
As the contracts which were let by the old Shell Committee are being completed and paid for, is or is not the payment being made directly by the Canadian Government?

Aly information upon that point-and I think it is correct-is this: the Canadian Government is not buying a single dpllar's worth of anything so far as the Imperial Munitions Board is concerned. This Board, presided over by Mr. Flavelle, issues its own cheques, and pay their obligations alike for those liabilities that were created before they came into being, but which -they assume by reason of their having taken over the responsibilities of the old Shell Committee, and for the new burdens which they themselves have created.
But the money comes from the Government of Canada.

It does not in any sense come from the Government or from the people of Canada. We lend money to the British Government and they lend money to us; it is a debtor and creditor transaction from start to finish.
The next point is the constitutional question: should this Parliament ask for an investigation if the principal whose money it has and to whom the agent is responsible not only does not ask for, but says he does not want an investigation?
Has the Imperial Government said that?
It has.
Through whom?
Air. Hiehens, representing the Minister of Munitions.
He does not profess to speak for the Imperial Government in the matter.
He did speak for them.
He speaks personally.

Then, Mr. Hiehens, speaking personally, though representing him-
ItEVISED EDITION

self as having the power of the Minister of Munitions, Mr. Lloyd George, told the Prime Minister of this country that Mr. D. A. Thomas or his successor had in Canada all the powers of the Minister of Munitions himself. Perhaps he did not know-I suggest that.
9	p.m. Has my hon. friend looked the facts, in the eye? Why do my hon. friends desire to make party capital of this matter? Why not be good enough Canadians to be proud ot what has been done? I am doing nothing more than reciting the facts as I understand them; I have no prejudices in the matter. I do. think, as a student, in a small way, of constitutional principles and the political history of our cwuntry, that two propositions are firmly established, namely, that we have no power to investigate the expenditure of other people's money in this country, and that, if the Government whose money it was says that it has no desire for investigation, we should respect its wishes. Tell me this: should we investigate the expenditures of the Hudson Bay Company in Canada for the French Govern-ernment, for the Russian Government, for the Italian Government, for the British Government? Should we investigate the expenditure of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for the rather large sums that they have expended for the British Government?

We appointed them
agents; why not?
We did not appoint them agents.
We appointed the Shell Committee.
No, we named them as being the persons who were fit to be agents, and the principal has said that he is well satisfied.
The Minister of Militia appointed them.
He says he did.
And they say that they reported to the minister once a week.

Certainly, in order that he who recommended the agent to the principal might know that his faith in the agent whom he had named had been warranted. Suppose the hon. member for St. John said to me: I should like to have an agent out your way to look after some matters for me. I say : I think Smith would make a

good man; my hon. friend says, very well, Smith makes no bargain, no sale, no purchases, without telegraphing the hon. member for St. John. I say: I have named you, Smith, as a fit person to be agent for Dr. Pugsley; I want you to report to me every week what you have done, in order that I may know that I have made no mistake in naming you and that my faith in your capacity as agent has not been unwarranted.

Suppose I were to name Smith in Calgary to do my business. Smith says: I will have to employ three clerks to attend to this business-Mr. Jones, Mr. Brown, and Mr. Robinson. I will appoint these gentlemen as my clerks to attend to this business which you have entrusted to me. Does my hon. friend say that afterwards Smith could not investigate the conduct. of the three clerks that he appointed?
Why, certainly; that is the very point I am trying to make.
Let me carry it a little further.

You had better go
back.

Not at all. The Minister of Militia, as representing the people of Canada, appointed this Shell Committee to look after the business with which he, as representing the people of Canada, was entrusted. All we ask is that the people of Canada shall be allowed to investigate the conduct of the eight or ten members of this Shell Committee whom the Minister of Militia appointed.
My hon. friend has got a little confused, which is indeed rather surprising. I must say that in all my long experience with the hon. gentleman I never saw Rim muddled so badly.

The matter is quite
clear in my own mind.
Well, it is a matter of expressing it, probably.
Probably so. If I could talk the one-hundredth part as fast as my hon. friend does, I should be all right.

I am bound to say that my hon. friend can always talk rapidly enough to disguise his real meaning.
* I leave the constitutional phase of the matter, and the next point I desire to make is this: is it expedient

from the national, not the political standpoint-that this investigation should be held?
It certainly is.

My hon. friend saye that it is. With that I join issue. He is only saying that in an academic sense to see if I have any reason for the 'faith that is in me. I urge that it is inexpedient for these reasons, (1) from the standpoint of manufacturing in this country; (2) from the standpoint of our credit; (3) because our energies should all be used for the war; and lastly that nothing will suffer by waiting, which is very important.
Let us see how the manufacturing interests are affected. Last summer I was in Paris, and while I was there, a gentleman representing Canadian manufacturers came to the hotel and asked me if I would endeavour to intercede with the Premier and with the Minister of War to say that Canadian boots were such as might safely be ordered by the French Government and worn by the French soldiers. I inquired, and this was the answer: It was explained to me that because of the damning given to the reputation of Canadian boots by men, such as the hon. member for Carleton and others of that type at the last session of Parliament Canadian boots and shoes were not held in high esteem in France. I /say to-day in this House that not les3 than $10,000,000 worth of boot and shoe business was lost to the Dominion of Canada by the slanderous attacks made upon them by the Opposition in this House. I say that in all seriousness. No statements or representations that could be made were sufficient to overcome the prejudice that had been created in the minds of those people by the attacks made in a committee of this House.
Further, when I was in London I picked up the Daily Chronicle. The Times, and the Morning Post, and the Daily Telegraph had been telling the people of England of the possibilities of Canada, and of how our business men might assist in the conduct of the war, and' I read an article signed by a man, whose name I forget, in which he said: what have we to expect from Canada in the matter of help in t'he war; they are such a corrupt bunch over there that at the last session of Parliament so and so took place. And, Sir, my country, and your country, and the country of the Canadian people was held up to the British people and to t'he citizens of the great Republic of France as a country which, in this great crisis of the world's history, thought more of dollars than of the fate of 100J
the Empire, and more of partyiem than of patriotism.

Is my hon. friend aware that the committee for the consideration of the question of boots was moved for- by the Prime Minister himself, and not at the instigation of any one on this side of the House?

I am aware of the fact that the Prime Minister, yielded to the unconscionable importunities and cries and howls of tale bearers. But if I know the Prime Minister, he is not going to see his country vilified and slandered a second time at the instance of the hon. member for Carleton and his friends.
You are keeping the lid on this time all right.

My hon. friend talks about keeping the lid on. Patriotism with him spells keeping the lid on. His idea of patriotism consists in advantage to a party; that is all. I say that when you are confronted with a situation such as this war has produced, we can at least afford to wait a day or two. What man in this House whose residence is burning, whose business is being destroyed, and the hose bursts, would stop putting out the fire because the hose bursts, to investigate the town council that bought the hose? I put that to the House and to the country. I ask the fathers whose sons are at the front whether or not they want this war stopped while the hon. member from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) investigate as to who is responsible for the hose. Is it not a lovely spectacle; is it not an elevating spectacle of Canadian patriotism to see the brains and the genius of one party of the State being used in the middle of a great war for the purpose of slandering, vilifying, and holding up to execration their fellow Canadians, lessening the respect with which they are held by the peoples of the world, destroying the proud position which we have attained by the greatness of our troops on the field of battle, and causing the name of Canadians to be a by-word and a reproach in the market places of the world. That is my hon. friend's idea of patriotism, but it does not reflect the genius of the Liberal party as represented by the people of this country, however much it may represent .the highest ideal of the hon. member for Carleton.
Let me go a step further. It hurts our credit. Who so avaricious as the money

lender in a neutral state? Who takes advantage of every opportunity to take the last cent of interest out of the country at war so much as the neutral state? I do not know, because I am riot sufficiently a student to express a sound opinion, but from the greatest financial men whom I saw in England, I learned that the economic side of this war is transcendently the most important. Some of them said they almost despaired of our ability to meet the great drains made on our financial resources. We are borrowers in the United States; we are borrowers at home. We are part of the British Empire, and our credit must suffer if the credit of the Empire suffers. In floating the Anglo-French loan, they pledged the credit of France and the credit of the British Emfpire, and here in this Parliament of ours, in this new democracy, there are men so little concerned with the tremendous issues of this war as to fritter away the time of the State and of Parliament by attacking the Shell Committee, which bought munitions of war to the satisfaction of the British Parliament, but which did not please a couple of hon. gentlemen. Is our credit thus to be destroyed? One-quarter of one per cent on our loans, one-half of one per cent more interest on the moneys we must borrow, means a charge upon the people of this country that, measured month by month for five years, will amount to $5,000,000 and, for ten years to a sufficient sum to enable us to complete great national undertakings, or to provide for the readjustment period after the war, or for larger pensions for those who are dependent. Is it a right thing to thus hurt our credit, is it right to thus destroy and injure the reputations of our manufacturers? I should like this to be placed on Hansard; one of the great purchasing agents for the Allies, representing a foreign government, said to me that Canadian manufactured goods were better than any goods he had bought upon the American continent. I was proud of it. Now, I am told that a committee is needed to investigate and hold up to scorn and obloquy the men who are devoting their energies and time to this work for the purpose of assisting in ending this war.
But that is not all. I should like to make this clear. You say: '"Why should we not hold- an investigation?" I say: Why should you not hold an investigattion later on if you want it? If the constitutional repuixements are met, and a dollar 0=1 expenditure goes through the public accounts, you are entitled to an investigation. If we pay out a dollar you can demand an

investigation. Who will be injured if an investigation is delayed?, Who stops in the midst of a conflagration to investigate who bought the hose? Do I understand it to be the policy of the Liberal party to say to the people of the British Empire: We want to stop^war until we find out if the agents of the Imperial Government did their duty? No, no. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition says no to that? Surely he says no. With his large experience and his great knowledge of the constitution and the political history of our country, he must say no to that. The position he took on the South African war question was sound absolutely from the const!-' tutional standpoint.
Do you realise what an investigation means? Let us concede that you have it. [Over three hundred concerns, large and small, would be affected.' With, a parliamentary committee sitting at- Ottawa men would be brought from Victoria, Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Medicine Hat, Winnipeg, Moosejaw, Saskatoon, Port Arthur, Fort William, St- John, Halifax, Orillia, every little town in the country, to attend this investigation. You, sirs, talk of delay. Axe you going to stop the wheels of Government and industry until you can get these little vaporings before the people of Canada? You are going to stop the highly skilled business of the country and these men are going to be dragged away from their businesses and brought here while an investigation is held. That is what is going to happen and you call that states-craft and patriotism. You cannot seriously mean that. Can a man like Colonel Cant-ley leave the operations at New Glasgow- for the purpose of coming here and sitting around listening to learned questions about steel being asked of him? Can the managers of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company come here and attend an investigation of this kind? What is to happen these great businesses while these men are here? Last year we saw the Militia Department disorganized while Parliament investigated boots. What are you going to do now? Not only are you going to disorganize and dislocate industry but, more, you are -going to place an intolerable burden and responsibility upon the Government while this investigation continues. I appeal to the patriotism, to the humanity, of the men of this House to say whether or not they are living up to the highest ideals of Canadianism when they say that the Prime Minister, already over.-weighted with matters of Government, is to have this added to the burden, if min-

isters of the Crown already overburdened with responsibility shall have this parliamentary investigation thrust upon them for ' the purpose of making a little cheap glory for a man like the hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B. Is that the idea that prevails in this House and throughout the country? I think it is not. I should like to say this in all seriousness; there is ample time for this matter to be dealt with when this war is over.
I alluded'-a few moments ago to the observations of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition. He pointed out that there had been dereliction of duty, that as a result there had been a shortage of shells upon the battlefield, that retreats of the enemy had not been followed up and that great vantages had not been pursued to the full. What does that mean? That means an inquiry into the operations of the war. Why should we undertake an inquiry, in the midst of the war, as to its operations? Does the right hon. gentleman say that, sitting here in all their wisdom, five or seven members of this Parliament can determine whether or not the Gallipoli operations were properly carried out? Can he say that at the battle of NeuVe Chapelle the failure of , munitions wras traceable to the failure of Canadian manufacturers? Can he say that at Loos the attack failed because of the shortage of Canadian munitions? Does he ask for an investigation into the operations of this great conflict? A few days ago Mr. Asquith refused absolutely to consider it. We all know the great discussion that has . taken place between Lord Kitchener and Lord French in relation to the failure of munitions at Neuve Chapelle. Mr. Asquith said at Newcastle that he had ample information from Lord, Kitchener himself that the supplies of munitions were double the demands that might be made upon them. In terms Lord Kitchener said that be had received this information from General French. It turned out that there were not supplies of munitions sufficient for carrying on the operations for five days. What happened? In Parliament an investigation was demanded and brushed aside lay Mr. Asquith as a petty piffling thing which could only be considered when the war was over. Though challenging the operations of Sir Ian Hamilton at Gallipoli, where thousands of Australians made the supreme sacrifice, the Australians, angry though they were, are yet still content to wait till the war is over, till the victory is won. The same is true of New Zealand, and the same is true in regard to operations
in France. General Joffre, the great commander-in-chief, has found it necessary to dismiss some of his generals, and he has dismissed them without an investigation, because the investigation can wait until the war is over. The British Government has dismissed and superseded generals who have been in charge of divisions and army corps. It is true that the British Government has wiped out the Shell Committee. It has appointed a Munitions Board, but on that Munitions Board it has appointed to membership two gentlemen who were members of the late Shell Committee. But, Sir, do hon. gentlemen for a single moment say that it is our dpty at this time to endeavour to hold a post mortem examination upon their conduct when no crime is charged, when they are said to be free from dishonesty in their condpet, and when all that can be said about them is that they have been negligent ?
Sir, I have a profound conviction that when this war is over and when an investigation into its conduct has been held alike in the Mother Country and in the overseas dominions, some reputations that are now looked upon as great will fall. I have a profound conviction, too, that men who have profited by the necessities of the state, who have washed their hands in blood money,, go to speak-they and their children's children-will be remembered with execrations and curses by the men who come after. But now is not the time, in the midst of this great eonflict, to cease our activities, to wear out our energies beating against the rock. The function and duty of the Opposition is fearlessly to oppose and boldly to criticise; but they can dothatconstruotively as well as destructively. Every thoughtful suggestion offered by an Opposition should be considered, and, if possible, acted upon by the Government of the day. In a great war, where unity of purpose is absolutely necessary, where cohesive and co-ordinated effort is demanded by every father, mother, wife, son and daughter within the state- oh, in such a war as this, let us show to the world the spectacle of a people united; determined that come what will, let it be for good or ill, we may be able to say when history is written that we have .neglected no opportunity, and overlooked no possibility; but that we have devoted our energies fearlessly, determinedly, and unitedly for the purpose of making victory assured, that liberty and freedom may continue among the sons of -men, and that

our civilization may be preserved to *posterity.

I will first deal with the Intercolonial railway, and I am pleased, tp be able to say that during the present year the Intercolonial has received its share of the increased business enjoyed by railways generally, so much so that the result has been that the current year will be the best in the history of the road. To put it in concrete form, our gross earnings at the end of December were increased by $1,191,000, while the increase in working expenses amounted to only ' $43,000. The particular items of economy which worked together for the above result are as follows: Fuel economy campaign, which-covers the cost of coal, loading on locomotives and economy in firing; engine house expenses Teduced by improved methods of handling work at round houses; closer supervision of stores and stores accounting; increased tonnage on freight trains due to the use of heavier locomotives made possible on account of strengthening bridges; great efficiency in Moncton and Riviere du Loup shops occasioned by re-organization of staff. To this should be added the economy that is being practised in every branch of the service on account of a desire of the officers and employees generally to make the Intercolonial a railway of which every man connected with its operation may be proud.
I am therefore glad to bear tribute to the fact that the various classes of employees on the road have been doing their best to make the operation of the Intercolonial as successful as that of privately-owned roads. Domestic Water Supply.
The construction of the Welland Ship Canal will interfere with the domestic water supply of several municipalities. This has been the subject of negotiations and conferences between the municipal representatives and Mr. Cochrane and his superintending engineer, and a tentative agreement has 'been entered into between the department and the different municipalities under which the department is to assume the cost of building a pipe line to carry water from Lake Erie to the reservoirs of the municipalities of Welland, Merritton, Thorold and St. Catharines, to supply pure water in place of the polluted water which will enter the canal through the Welland river, when that river is absorbed in the canal system. The department assumes the cost of building the pipe line, an$ the municipalities are to pay a fixed annual rental for the same. No actual work has been done in connection with the proposed pipe line, although experiments are being made on a three hundred foot piece of thirty-inch reinforced concrete pipe, which is being 'built at Port Colborne. Should these experiments be successful, this system of construction will be recommended for adoption. It will take about two years to complete the line after active operations on it are begun.
The work( in connection with these ship canal contracts and the letting of further contracts is not being pressed by the Gov- , eminent as fast as probably it might have been had war conditions not rendered advisable the keeping of departmental expenditures as low as possible while the conflict continues. Although this may delay the completion of the work for a time, it is felt to be the proper course to pursue.
St. Peter's Canal.
The improvement of this canal, as designed, consists of the construction of a new lock and entrance at the Atlantic end. v The contract was let to W. H. Weller, of St. Catharines, and work was commenced in May of 1912 and continued through the seasons of 1912 and 1913. As a result of new borings taken in February, 1913, to more accurately determine the surface of the rock, it was found that the greater part of the new lock, as designed, did not rest on solid rock. It was considered advisable, therefore, to adopt a new location for the lock and make a radical change in the entrance. A supplemental agreement to the contract was accordingly entered into in June of 1914 under authority of order in council, and in accordance with conditions as explained by me to the House on May 29, 1914. (Hansard proceedings, page 4480). The changes decided upon necessitated the closing of the canal to navigation for one year and work was immediately undertaken for the unwatering of the canal. On the outbreak of war, however, it was considered advisable to keep the canal open for navigation, and the contractor was obliged to stop all work in connection with the unwatering. In March of 1915, Mr. Cochrane considered that the time had come when the canal might safely be closed so that the construction work might be completed, and since that time satisfactory progress has been made.

Trent Canal.
This canal is familiar history to most members of this House, having formed a



part of the annual Budget of the Minister of Railways and Canals for a couple of generations. It is very satisfactory to know that our engineers hope to have that portion of the canal between the city of Peterborough and lake Ontario known as the Ontario-Rice Lake division completed and open to navigation by the spring of 1917. The work remaining to be done consists of the dredging out of river channels. All the structures have been completed except the reconstruction of the Grand Trunk railway bridge at Campbellford, the completion of a few sluices in dam No. 10, which have been held back pending the execution of the bridge reconstruction, and the hanging of lock gates between Glen Ross and Healey falls. Upon completion vessels having a draft of eight feet will have access to Peterborough from the Great Lakes. This will be an event of considerable importance to the communities along that section of the canal. The total estimated cost of the Ontario-Rice Lake division is $7,660,000, of which about $750,000 remains to be expended.
Negotiations have been concluded with officials of the railway for an agreement whereby the bridge will be reconstructed as a high level structure instead of a swing span, as originally proposed, and the work will be proceeded with this season.
On the Georgian bay end, of the Severn division, the Port Severn lock and the approaches thereto have been completed giving access to Gloucester pool from Georgian bay. Good progress has been made upon sections Nos. 2 and 3, which provide for the canalization of the upper reaches of the river. Owing to the war we have held back the letting of section No- 1, which will be necessary for through navigation. The total estimated cost of the Severn division is $3,575,000, of which work to the value of about $1,250,000 has been done!
The construction of tne Trent canal has resulted in the development of a 'large amount of water-power, which will be of very great assistance in the industrial upbuilding of Eastern Ontario. In fact, this electrical development is the key to the situation. Unfortunately, some years ago these powers were leased to parties at nominal rentals on the understanding, as I am informed, that they were to be developed and the people would enjoy the benefits of this development. Now these powers have been alienated but the people are not obtaining the benefits they expected. For instance, some of these powers have now been under lease for ten

or fifteen years and no development whatever has taken place. The people of Eastern Ontario must have electric power, and I understand negotiations are on at the present time between the Ontario Government and the lessees of these water powers, and the Ontario Government is trying to airrange that these powers shall be developed. If these negotiations do not succeed, and should it become necessary, I shall recommend that a Dill be brought down cancelling these leases and returning these powers to the Crown so that the people may have the benefit of a new deal.
